entries.41.1: Having dismissed the bears and vanaras and rakshasas, the mighty-armed Rama took his pleasure happily with his brothers.
entries.41.2: Then in the afternoon Raghava, with his brothers, heard a sweet voice speaking from the sky:
entries.41.3: 'Look upon me with a gentle face, gentle Rama. Know me, lord, to be the Pushpaka, come from Kubera's dwelling.
entries.41.4: 'Understanding your command, I went to his house to wait upon him, best of men; and he said this to me:
entries.41.5: '"You have been won by the great-souled king Raghava, who slew in battle the unassailable Ravana, lord of rakshasas.
entries.41.6: '"And I too have the highest joy in the slaying of that evil-souled Ravana, with his hosts and his sons and his kinsmen.
entries.41.7: '"So you have been won by that supreme soul Rama in Lanka. Bear him then, gentle one; this is my command to you.
entries.41.8: '"For this is my highest wish, that you should bear the delight of the Raghus, who is the refuge of the world. Go, free of fever."
entries.41.9: 'So, understanding the command of the great-souled giver of wealth, I have come into your presence. Receive me without doubt.
entries.41.10: 'By the command of the giver of wealth and by my own power I shall move unseen by all beings, obeying your word.'
entries.41.11: Being addressed thus by the Pushpaka, the mighty Rama, seeing that chariot come again, said to it:
entries.41.12: 'If it is so, then you are welcome, Pushpaka, best of chariots. With the giver of wealth agreeing, no fault of conduct will fall upon us.'
entries.41.13: Then the mighty-armed Raghava honoured the Pushpaka with parched grain and flowers and fragrant incense,
entries.41.14: and said: 'Go now, and come when I remember you. Gentle one, in your going upon the path of the siddhas, bring no one to grief. And let there be no hindrance for you as you go where you wish.'
entries.41.15: 'So be it' — and being honoured and dismissed by Rama, the Pushpaka went then from that place toward the quarter it desired.
entries.41.16: And when that holy Pushpaka had thus vanished, Bharata with joined palms said to the delight of the Raghus:
entries.41.17: 'While you rule, hero, signs of many kinds are seen — the voices of more than human beings are heard again and again.
entries.41.18: 'And a full month and more has gone by with no sickness among creatures, Raghava, and death does not come even to the aged.
entries.41.19: 'Women bear children without disease and men are strong of body; and the joy of the people of the city grows greater, king.
entries.41.20: 'The rain-god sends rain in its season, letting fall water that is nectar; and the winds blow with a touch that is pleasant, kindly and auspicious.
entries.41.21: '"May such a king endure and never pass away" — so the people of the city and the country say, king.'
entries.41.22: Hearing these most sweet words spoken by Bharata, Rama, best of kings, was filled with joy.
entries.42.1: Then, having dismissed the gold-adorned Pushpaka, the mighty-armed Rama entered the ashoka grove.
entries.42.2: It was adorned on every side with sandal and aloe and mango, with tunga and kaleyaka, and with forests of deodar;
entries.42.3: shining with champaka, ashoka, punnaga, madhuka, jackfruit and asana, and with parijatas bright as smokeless flame;
entries.42.4: covered with lodhra and nipa and arjuna, with naga and saptaparna and atimuktaka, with mandara and plantain thickets and a web of creepers;
entries.42.5: adorned with priyangu and kadamba and with bakula too, with rose-apple and pomegranate and kovidara;
entries.42.6: always lovely with flowers and pleasing with fruit, with young shoots and leaves possessed of divine fragrance and taste;
entries.42.7: and with divine trees set in order by craftsmen, rich in fair leaf and flower and thronged with intoxicated bees;
entries.42.8: adorned by cuckoos and bhringarajas and birds of many colours, made wonderful by hundreds of mango trees for its ornament.
entries.42.9: Some of the trees there shone like gold, some like tongues of flame, and others like dark collyrium.
entries.42.10: There were fragrant flowers and garlands of many kinds, and long pools of many shapes filled with the finest water,
entries.42.11: with steps of ruby and floors of crystal within, with groves of open lotus and lily and made lovely by chakravakas,
entries.42.12: loud with datyuhas and parrots, sounding with swans and cranes, and adorned by flowering trees upon their banks,
entries.42.13: set about with walls of many kinds and with slabs of stone. And in that woodland, like beryl,
entries.42.14: the grass spread everywhere and the groves stood in flower. And of those trees vying with one another in blossom,
entries.42.15: the fallen flowers dappled the rocks as the stars dapple the sky. As Indra has his Nandana and Brahma his Chaitraratha,
entries.42.16: such was that grove of Rama's dwelling, with many seats and pavilions and set about with bowers of creeper.
entries.42.17: Entering that rich ashoka grove, the delight of the Raghus, upon a fair seat strewn with heaps of flowers
entries.42.18: and spread with kusha grass, Rama sat down. And taking Sita by the hand, that pure and honeyed wine
entries.42.19: Kakutstha gave her to drink, as Purandara gives to Shachi. And well-dressed flesh and fruit of many kinds
entries.42.20: the attendants brought swiftly for Rama's eating. And those skilled in dance and song danced before the king —
entries.42.21: young and beautiful women, given to wine, lovely to the heart; and Rama, best of those who take delight,
entries.42.22: while those women skilled in dance and song danced before Kakutstha, lovely to the heart,
entries.42.23: that soul of dharma, richly adorned, gave them pleasure daily. And seated there with Sita he shone
entries.42.24: as Vasishtha shines in splendour seated with Arundhati. So Rama, filled with joy, with Sita who was like a daughter of the gods,
entries.42.25: took his pleasure with Vaidehi day after day as a god might. And as those two, Sita and Raghava, sported thus a long while,
entries.42.26: that auspicious season of the cool weather, ever giving delight, passed away, and the coming of the cold was gone for those who had enjoyed pleasures of many kinds.
entries.42.27: In the forenoon that knower of dharma performed the works of dharma according to dharma, and spent the remaining half of the day within his inner apartments.
entries.42.28: And Sita too, having performed the morning rites for the gods, paid honour to all her husband's mothers without distinction.
entries.42.29: Then she went to Rama, wearing wonderful ornaments and garments, as Shachi goes to the thousand-eyed one seated in the third heaven.
entries.42.30: And seeing his wife endowed with auspicious marks, Raghava was filled with joy beyond compare and said, 'Well, well!'
entries.42.31: And he said to Sita of the fair hips, who was like a daughter of the gods: 'The gaining of a child has come to me through you, Vaidehi.
entries.42.32: 'What do you wish, fair one? What desire of yours shall be fulfilled?' And Vaidehi, smiling, said these words to Rama:
entries.42.33: 'I wish to see the holy groves of penance, Raghava — of the sages of fierce splendour who dwell upon Ganga's bank,
entries.42.34: 'who live on fruit and root, and to spend some time at their feet, god. This is my highest wish, that among those who eat root and fruit
entries.42.35: 'I might dwell even for one night in that grove of penance, Kakutstha.' And Rama, whose deeds are done without effort, promised, saying, 'So it shall be. Be confident, Vaidehi; tomorrow you shall go, without a doubt.'
entries.42.36: Having spoken thus to Maithili, the daughter of Janaka, Kakutstha went out into the middle court surrounded by his friends.
entries.43.1: There, as the king sat, discerning men waited upon him, makers of merriment with stories of many kinds on every side —
entries.43.2: Vijaya and Madhumatta, Kashyapa, Mangala and Kuta, Suraja, Kaliya, Bhadra, Dantavakra and Sumagadha.
entries.43.3: These told stories of many kinds mixed with jesting, in gladness, to the great-souled Raghava.
entries.43.4: Then in the course of some story Raghava said, 'What talk is going about in the city, Bhadra, and in the countryside?
entries.43.5: 'What do the people of the city and the country say about me? And what about Sita, and what about Bharata and Lakshmana?
entries.43.6: 'And what about Shatrughna, and what about my mother Kaikeyi? For kings come to be spoken of, and even in the finest kingdom.'
entries.43.7: Being addressed thus by Rama, Bhadra said with joined palms: 'The talk that goes about among the citizens is auspicious, king.
entries.43.8: 'Chiefly, gentle one, it is this victory won by the slaying of Dashagriva that the citizens tell of in your city, bull among men.'
entries.43.9: Being told this by Bhadra, Raghava said: 'Tell it truly and all of it, leaving nothing out.
entries.43.10: 'Hearing the words the citizens speak, good and ill, I shall now do what is good and not do what is ill.
entries.43.11: 'Tell it confidently, without fear and without fever — how the citizens speak, and in the countryside too.'
entries.43.12: Being addressed thus by Raghava, Bhadra with joined palms and full attention answered that mighty-armed one with well-chosen words:
entries.43.13: 'Hear, king, what the citizens say of good and ill at the crossroads, in the markets and streets, in the woods and the groves.
entries.43.14: '"Rama has done what was hard to do — the binding of a bridge over the ocean, never heard of before by any, not even by the gods with the danavas.
entries.43.15: '"And the unassailable Ravana was slain with his forces and his mounts; and the vanaras and bears and even the rakshasas were brought under his sway.
entries.43.16: '"But having slain Ravana in battle and brought Sita back, Raghava put his anger behind him and brought her into his own house again.
entries.43.17: '"What sort of pleasure can there be in his heart in enjoying that Sita, who was carried off before by Ravana by force, taken into his lap,
entries.43.18: '"who was brought to Lanka and stayed in the ashoka grove and fell into the power of the rakshasas? How does Rama not loathe her?
entries.43.19: '"So we too shall have to bear the same in our own wives. For as the king does, so the people follow after him."
entries.43.20: 'Such are the many things the citizens say, king, and in all the cities and in the countryside too.'
entries.43.21: Hearing that speech, Raghava, sorely stricken, said to all his friends, 'Do you also say this of me?'
entries.43.22: And all of them bowed their heads to the ground and saluted him and answered the grieving Raghava, 'It is so, and there is no doubt of it.'
entries.43.23: Hearing that word spoken by them all, Kakutstha, destroyer of foes, then dismissed his companions.
entries.44.1: Having dismissed his company of friends and settled the matter in his mind, Raghava said this to the doorkeeper who sat nearby:
entries.44.2: 'Bring quickly Sumitra's son Lakshmana of auspicious marks, and the greatly blessed Bharata, and the unconquered Shatrughna.'
entries.44.3: Hearing Rama's word, the doorkeeper set his palms upon his head, went to Lakshmana's house and entered unhindered.
entries.44.4: Saluting that great one and with joined palms he said: 'The king wishes to see you; go there, and do not delay.'
entries.44.5: Hearing Raghava's command, Sumitra's son said, 'Very well,' and mounting his chariot went swiftly to Raghava's house.
entries.44.6: Seeing Lakshmana go, the doorkeeper went to Bharata and, saluting him there with joined palms,
entries.44.7: said, bowing in courtesy, 'The king wishes to see you.' And Bharata, hearing that word of Rama's from the doorkeeper,
entries.44.8: rose at once from his seat and went on foot, mighty though he was. Seeing Bharata go, the doorkeeper hastened with joined palms
entries.44.9: to Shatrughna's house and said, 'Come, best of the Raghus; the king wishes to see you.
entries.44.10: 'Lakshmana has gone before, and the renowned Bharata.' Hearing his words, Shatrughna rose from his high seat,
entries.44.11: bowed his head to the earth and went to where Raghava was. And the doorkeeper returned and with joined palms announced to Rama that all his brothers were come.
entries.44.12: Hearing that the princes had come, his senses troubled with care, with his face bent down and his mind wretched, he said to the doorkeeper:
entries.44.13: 'Bring the princes swiftly into my presence. In them is my life; they are my dear breath.'
entries.44.14: Being commanded by the lord of men, those princes, splendid as Shakra, came in bowing low with joined palms and with composed minds.
entries.44.15: And they saw his face like the moon seized by a planet, like the sun at twilight bereft of its brightness;
entries.44.16: and seeing the eyes of the wise Rama full of tears and his face like a lotus whose beauty is gone,
entries.44.17: they swiftly bowed their heads to Rama's feet and stood there all composed; and Rama's tears fell.
entries.44.18: And that mighty one raised them up with both his arms and embraced them, and saying, 'Sit upon the seats,' he spoke these words:
entries.44.19: 'You are my all, lords of men; you are my life. And it is the kingdom you have made that I rule.
entries.44.20: 'You are versed in the meaning of the scriptures and settled in understanding. Together, lords of men, you must consider this matter of mine.'
entries.44.21: As Kakutstha spoke so, all of them gave their whole attention, and were troubled in mind, wondering what the king would say.
entries.45.1: As they all sat there with wretched hearts, Kakutstha spoke these words with a dry mouth:
entries.45.2: 'Hear me, all of you, and may it be well with you; do not take it otherwise. Hear what talk goes about among the citizens concerning Sita.
entries.45.3: 'A great and hateful ill-report of me goes about among the citizens and among the people of the country, and it cuts my vitals.
entries.45.4: 'I was born in the line of the great-souled Ikshvakus, and Sita too was born in the good line of the great-souled Janakas.
entries.45.5: 'You know, gentle one, how Sita was carried off by Ravana in the lonely forest of Dandaka, and how he was destroyed by me.
entries.45.6: 'And then this thought arose in me concerning Janaka's daughter: how should I bring to my city this Sita who has dwelt there?
entries.45.7: 'Then Sita entered the fire for proof, Sumitra's son, before your very eyes; and the bearer of oblations declared Maithili sinless before the gods, and the wind that moves in the sky said the same,
entries.45.8: 'and the moon and the sun proclaimed her so of old in the presence of the gods, and before all the sages the daughter of Janaka was declared sinless.
entries.45.9: 'Thus, being proved pure in conduct in the presence of gods and gandharvas, she was placed in my hand by Mahendra himself in the island of Lanka.
entries.45.10: 'And my own inmost soul knows the glorious Sita to be pure. Therefore I took Vaidehi and came to Ayodhya.
entries.45.11: 'But this great reproach and this grief lie in my heart. The ill-report among the citizens and the people of the country is very great.
entries.45.12: 'Of whatever being in the world an ill fame is sung, so long as that report is spoken he falls into the lower worlds.
entries.45.13: 'Ill fame is blamed by the gods, and glory is honoured in the worlds. It is for glory that all great souls make their endeavour.
entries.45.14: 'I would give up my life, bulls among men, or you yourselves, in fear of that reproach — how much more then the daughter of Janaka?
entries.45.15: 'Therefore look upon me as fallen into an ocean of sorrow. I see no being with a grief greater than this.
entries.45.16: 'Tomorrow at dawn, Sumitra's son, mount the chariot driven by Sumantra, take Sita upon it and set her down beyond the borders of the kingdom.
entries.45.17: 'On the far bank of Ganga is the divine hermitage of the great-souled Valmiki, upon the bank of the Tamasa.
entries.45.18: 'Leave her there in a lonely place, delight of the Raghus, and come back swiftly; may it be well with you, and do as I say.
entries.45.19: 'And nothing whatever is to be said in answer to this on Sita's behalf. Go therefore, Sumitra's son, and let there be no debating it.
entries.45.20: 'For if this is prevented by you, it will be the greatest displeasure to me. I lay upon you all the oath of my arms and of my life.
entries.45.21: 'Whoever should speak in the middle of my words to persuade me in any way, they shall be counted my enemies always, for hindering what I desire.
entries.45.22: 'Honour me, then, if you stand within my command. Let Sita be taken from here today; do as I say.
entries.45.23: 'For she said to me before that she wished to see the hermitages upon Ganga's bank; and let that desire of hers be fulfilled.'
entries.45.24: Having spoken thus, Kakutstha, his face covered with tears, that soul of dharma went within, surrounded by his brothers,
entries.45.25: his heart clinging to grief, and sighed like an elephant.
entries.46.1: Then, when the night had passed, Lakshmana with a wretched heart said these words to Sumantra with a dry mouth:
entries.46.2: 'Charioteer, yoke the horses swiftly to the best of chariots, and make a well-spread seat from the royal house for Sita.
entries.46.3: 'For by the king's word Sita is to be taken by me to the hermitage of those whose deeds are holy. Let the chariot be brought quickly.'
entries.46.4: And Sumantra said, 'So be it,' and brought a chariot yoked with the finest horses, most fair to look upon and well spread with a comfortable couch,
entries.46.5: and said to Sumitra's son, the increaser of his friends' honour, 'The chariot has come, lord; let what is to be done be done.'
entries.46.6: Being addressed thus by Sumantra, Lakshmana entered the royal house and, coming to Sita, that bull among men said:
entries.46.7: 'You asked a boon of the king, lady, and it was promised by the king; and I am commanded to take you to the hermitages.
entries.46.8: 'By the command of our king, Vaidehi, I am to take you swiftly to the auspicious hermitages of the sages upon Ganga's bank, in that forest frequented by the sages.'
entries.46.9: Being addressed thus by the great-souled Lakshmana, Vaidehi felt a joy beyond compare and was glad to go.
entries.46.10: Taking costly garments and jewels of many kinds, Vaidehi made ready to go, saying:
entries.46.11: 'These ornaments I shall give to the wives of the sages, and costly garments too and wealth of many kinds.'
entries.46.12: And Sumitra's son said, 'So be it,' and setting Maithili upon the chariot he went with swift horses, remembering Rama's command.
entries.46.13: And Sita then said to Lakshmana, the increaser of fortune: 'I see many ill omens, delight of the Raghus.
entries.46.14: 'My eye twitches today and my body trembles; and my heart, Sumitra's son, I feel to be unwell.
entries.46.15: 'And there is a great restlessness in me and the greatest unease; and I see the earth as though it were empty, wide-eyed one.
entries.46.16: 'Is it well with that brother of yours, lover of your brother? And with all my husband's mothers, hero, without distinction?
entries.46.17: 'And is it well with the beings of the city and the country?' So Sita with joined palms besought the gods.
entries.46.18: Then Lakshmana, hearing this, bowed his head to Maithili and said 'It is well,' seeming glad, though his heart was drying within him.
entries.46.19: Then coming to a lodging in a hermitage upon the bank of the Gomati, Sumitra's son rose again at dawn and said to the charioteer:
entries.46.20: 'Yoke the chariot swiftly; today I shall bear upon my head the water of Bhagirathi as Tryambaka did upon the mountain.'
entries.46.21: And he yoked four horses swift as thought to the chariot with their traces, and the charioteer said with joined palms to Vaidehi, 'Mount.'
entries.46.22: And at the charioteer's word she mounted that best of chariots — Sita with Sumitra's son and with the wise Sumantra.
entries.46.23: And that wide-eyed one came to Ganga, destroyer of sin. Then, having gone half a day, upon reaching the waters of Bhagirathi
entries.46.24: Lakshmana looked upon them and wept aloud in his wretchedness.
entries.46.25: And Sita, greatly troubled at seeing Lakshmana in distress, that knower of dharma said, 'Why is this weeping of yours?
entries.46.26: 'Coming to the bank of Jahnavi has long been my desire. Why at this hour of joy do you make me sorrowful, Lakshmana?
entries.46.27: 'You are always at Rama's side, bull among men. Has this grief come upon you because you are parted from him for two nights?
entries.46.28: 'Rama is dearer to me than life itself, Lakshmana, and yet I do not grieve so. Do not be so childish.
entries.46.29: 'Carry me across the Ganga and show me the ascetics. Then I shall give the sages garments and ornaments.
entries.46.30: 'And having made obeisance to the great sages as is fitting, and having spent one night there, we shall go back again to the city.
entries.46.31: 'For my mind too hastens to see Rama of the lotus-petal eyes, with the chest of a lion and the slender waist, best of those who take delight.'
entries.46.32: Hearing those words of hers, Lakshmana, slayer of enemy heroes, wiped his fair eyes and called the boatmen.
entries.46.33: And the fishermen said with joined palms, 'This boat is ready.'
entries.46.34: And wishing to cross Ganga, Lakshmana mounted that fair boat; and with a composed mind he brought her across the Ganga.
entries.47.1: Then the younger brother of Raghava, having first set Maithili aboard, mounted himself that broad and well-appointed boat of the Nishadas.
entries.47.2: And Lakshmana, burning with grief, told Sumantra to wait there with the chariot, and said to the boatman, 'Go.'
entries.47.3: Then, coming to the further bank of Bhagirathi, Lakshmana said to Maithili with joined palms, drowned in tears:
entries.47.4: 'A great dart lies in my heart, Vaidehi, in that by this cause my wise elder brother has been made a matter for men's reproach.
entries.47.5: 'Better for me today were death, or whatever may be beyond death, than to be appointed to this deed which the world condemns.
entries.47.6: 'Be gracious to me, fair one, and do not hold me a sinner.' And saying this, Lakshmana with joined palms fell upon the ground.
entries.47.7: Seeing him weeping with joined palms and longing for his own death, Maithili was greatly troubled and said to Lakshmana:
entries.47.8: 'What is this? I do not understand. Tell me truly, Lakshmana. I do not see you well. Is it well with the king?
entries.47.9: 'If you have been bound by the king with an oath, so that you are in such torment, then speak it before me; I command you.'
entries.47.10: Being pressed thus by Vaidehi, Lakshmana with a wretched heart, his face bent down, said these words in a voice choked with tears:
entries.47.11: 'Hearing in the midst of the assembly the most dreadful ill-report in the city and the country concerning you, daughter of Janaka, Rama with a burning heart gave me his command and went within, without telling you.
entries.47.12: 'Those things are not to be spoken by me before you, lady, which the king took into his heart and put his anger behind him.
entries.47.13: 'So you have been abandoned by the king, though blameless, in my presence, in fear of the citizens' reproach. Do not take it otherwise, lady.
entries.47.14: 'You are to be left by me near these hermitages. This is the king's command; and it was your own longing besides.
entries.47.15: 'This is the penance-grove of the brahmarshis upon Jahnavi's bank, holy and lovely; do not grieve, auspicious one.
entries.47.16: 'The dear friend of my father king Dasharatha, that bull among sages, the most excellent brahmin, the greatly renowned Valmiki,
entries.47.17: 'lives here. Coming to the shade of that great one's feet, dwell there in ease, daughter of Janaka, intent upon fasting and singleness of mind.
entries.47.18: 'Holding fast to the dharma of a faithful wife and keeping Rama always in your heart, lady, so doing, the highest good shall be yours.'
entries.48.1: Hearing that dreadful word of Lakshmana, the daughter of Janaka, Vaidehi, fell to the ground in the deepest despair.
entries.48.2: And for a moment she lay as though senseless, her eyes brimming with tears; and then the daughter of Janaka said to Lakshmana in a wretched voice:
entries.48.3: 'Surely this body of mine was made by the Ordainer for sorrow, Lakshmana; for today my life appears to me a very image of sorrow.
entries.48.4: 'What sin did I do before, and whom did I part from his wife, that I, pure in conduct and a faithful wife, have been abandoned by the king?
entries.48.5: 'Before this, Sumitra's son, I dwelt in the hermitages of the forest following Rama's feet, and passed my life in sorrow.
entries.48.6: 'How then, gentle one, shall I dwell in a hermitage now, left thus alone? And to whom shall I tell my sorrow, sunk in sorrow as I am?
entries.48.7: 'What shall I say to the sages — for what fault the great-souled Raghava abandoned me?
entries.48.8: 'I would give up my life this very day, Sumitra's son, in the waters of Jahnavi; but by that the royal line of my husband would be destroyed.
entries.48.9: 'Do as you are commanded, Sumitra's son; leave me who am fit only for sorrow. Stand within the king's command, and hear this word of mine too.
entries.48.10: 'Salute all my husband's mothers without distinction, with joined palms and with your head bowed to their feet, and tell the king that it is well with me.
entries.48.11: 'Bowing your head, offer my salutation to them all, Lakshmana; and to the king, who is intent upon dharma, say this also:
entries.48.12: '"You know well, Raghava, that Sita is in truth pure, joined with the highest devotion and ever seeking your good.
entries.48.13: '"Fearing dishonour among the people, hero, you abandoned me. And that reproach which would fall upon you, arising from the ill-report — it is mine to take away, for you are my highest refuge."
entries.48.14: 'And say to the king, who is intent upon dharma: "As you bear yourself toward your brothers, so bear yourself always toward your people.
entries.48.15: '"This is your highest dharma, and from it comes glory beyond compare.
entries.48.16: '"Do that, king, by which the people may attain happiness through dharma. I do not grieve for my own body, bull among men.
entries.48.17: '"You have done according to the reproach of the citizens, delight of the Raghus. For a woman the husband is her god, the husband her kinsman, the husband her teacher.
entries.48.18: '"Therefore what pleases the husband is to be done above all, even at the cost of life."' Speak this message of mine to Rama, Lakshmana.
entries.48.19: 'And now look upon me, whose time is upon me, and go.' As Sita spoke thus, Lakshmana with a wretched heart
entries.48.20: bowed his head to the earth and could not speak a word. And going round her from left to right and weeping aloud,
entries.48.21: after brooding a moment he said to her, 'What more will you say to me, fair one? I have never before looked upon your face, sinless one; I have seen only your feet.
entries.48.22: 'How then shall I look upon you here in this forest, bereft of Rama?' And saying this, he saluted her and boarded the boat again.
entries.48.23: Boarding it and urging the boatman on, and coming to the further shore weighed down with the burden of grief,
entries.48.24: as though stupefied with sorrow, he mounted the chariot swiftly. And turning again and again to look, he saw Sita standing helpless,
entries.48.25: writhing upon the further shore; and Lakshmana went his way. And looking again and again at the chariot going far off, and at Lakshmana, grief came upon the troubled Sita.
entries.48.26: And she, bowed down beneath the weight of sorrow, glorious and whose wealth was her glory, not seeing her lord, wept aloud in that forest loud with the cries of peacocks, that faithful wife given over to grief.
entries.49.1: Seeing Sita weeping, the sons of the sages there ran to where the venerable Valmiki of keen mind was.
entries.49.2: Saluting the sage's feet, the sages' sons told the great sage all the sound of her weeping:
entries.49.3: 'We have never seen such a one before, venerable one. She seems the wife of some great soul; she is like Shri, but weeps with a face distraught with grief.
entries.49.4: 'Come and see her, venerable one; she is like a goddess fallen from the sky. Upon the bank of the river, venerable one, some excellent woman is in sorrow.
entries.49.5: 'We have seen her weeping, sunk deep in grief. She is not fit for sorrow or grief, yet she is alone, wretched and helpless.
entries.49.6: 'We do not think her even human. Fitting honour should be shown to her. She is near the hermitage and has come to you for refuge.
entries.49.7: 'That virtuous one seeks a protector; venerable one, you should protect her.' Hearing their words, that knower of dharma settled it in his mind,
entries.49.8: and having gained the eye of penance he went to where Maithili was. And seeing that great-minded one going, his disciples followed him; and that great-minded one, going a little way on foot,
entries.49.9: took a fair guest-offering and came to Jahnavi's bank. And there he saw Sita, the beloved wife of Raghava, sitting helpless.
entries.49.10: To that Sita, afflicted by the burden of sorrow, Valmiki, bull among sages, said in sweet words, as though gladdening her by his splendour:
entries.49.11: 'You are the daughter-in-law of Dasharatha, the beloved queen of Rama, the daughter of King Janaka. You are welcome, faithful wife.
entries.49.12: 'I knew of your coming beforehand by my meditation upon dharma, and the whole cause of it has become clear in my heart.
entries.49.13: 'All concerning you is known to me truly, greatly blessed one. Whatever passes in the three worlds, I know it all.
entries.49.14: 'By the eye won through penance I know you sinless, Sita. Be at ease, Vaidehi; you are now in my keeping.
entries.49.15: 'Near my hermitage dwell women ascetics established in penance. They will cherish you always, my child, as a cow her calf.
entries.49.16: 'Take this guest-offering, confident and free of fever. Think that you have come to your own house, and do not grieve.'
entries.49.17: Hearing that most wonderful speech of the sage, Sita bowed her head to his feet and said with joined palms, 'So be it.'
entries.49.18: And as the sage went back, Sita followed behind him with joined palms.
entries.49.19: Seeing the sage coming with Vaidehi, the wives of the sages came to him filled with gladness and said these words:
entries.49.20: 'Welcome, best of sages; you come after long. We all salute you. Tell us, what shall we do?'
entries.49.21: Hearing those words of theirs, Valmiki said: 'This Sita has come here, the wife of the wise Rama.
entries.49.22: 'She is the daughter-in-law of Dasharatha and the virtuous daughter of Janaka. Being sinless, she has been abandoned by her husband, and she is to be cherished by me always.
entries.49.23: 'Let you all look upon her with the highest affection. For my sake and by my word let her be especially honoured of you.'
entries.49.24: And having thus again and again given Vaidehi into their keeping, that greatly renowned one of great penance returned to his own hermitage surrounded by his disciples.
entries.50.1: Seeing Maithili Sita brought into the hermitage, Lakshmana with a wretched heart fell into dreadful anguish,
entries.50.2: and that one of great splendour said to Sumantra, the charioteer skilled in counsel: 'See, charioteer, Rama's sorrow born of Sita's sorrow.
entries.50.3: 'What sorrow could be greater than this for Raghava — that he has cast off his wife, the daughter of Janaka, pure in conduct?
entries.50.4: 'It is clear to me, charioteer, that this life of Raghava's without Vaidehi is by fate alone; for fate is hard to overpass.
entries.50.5: 'For Raghava, who in his anger could slay the gods with the gandharvas, and the asuras with the rakshasas, follows after fate.
entries.50.6: 'Before this, at his father's word, Rama dwelt in the lonely forest of Dandaka nine years and five in that great wood.
entries.50.7: 'And now more grievous still is this banishment of Sita, on the hearing of the citizens' words; it seems to me a cruel thing.
entries.50.8: 'Upon what dharma does it rest, charioteer, this deed that takes away his fame, done against Maithili at the word of citizens who speak meanly?'
entries.50.9: Hearing these many words spoken by Lakshmana, the wise Sumantra said this with reverence:
entries.50.10: 'You should not grieve for Maithili, Sumitra's son. This was seen long ago by brahmins in your father's presence, Lakshmana.
entries.50.11: '"Rama shall surely have his share of happiness, though much given to sorrow; and that mighty-armed one shall certainly know separation from those he loves.
entries.50.12: '"He shall abandon you and Maithili, and Shatrughna and Bharata both, that soul of dharma, that great one, after a long time."
entries.50.13: 'This is not to be spoken to you, Sumitra's son, nor to Bharata — that word which the king spoke of you, which Durvasa uttered.
entries.50.14: 'And in the presence of a great assembly and in mine, bull among men, that word was spoken by the sage, and in Vasishtha's presence.
entries.50.15: 'Hearing the sage's word, that best of men said to me, "Charioteer, this must never anywhere be spoken by you before people."
entries.50.16: 'And that word of that guardian of the world I have kept with full care; and it should never be made false — such is my judgement, gentle one.
entries.50.17: 'In every way it should not be spoken by me before you, gentle one. Yet if you have the desire to hear it, let it be heard, delight of the Raghus.
entries.50.18: 'Though I was bound before by the king when he told me this secret, still I shall tell it; for fate is hard to overpass.
entries.50.19: 'It is by that fate that this sorrow, joined with grief, has come. But it is not to be spoken by you to Bharata, nor in Shatrughna's presence.'
entries.50.20: Hearing that great speech of his with its words of deep meaning, Sumitra's son said to the charioteer, 'Tell me what is true.'
entries.51.1: Being pressed thus by the great-souled Lakshmana, the charioteer began to speak that word which the sage had uttered.
entries.51.2: 'Long ago a great sage named Durvasa, the son of Atri, dwelt through the rainy season in the holy hermitage of Vasishtha.
entries.51.3: 'And your father of great splendour and great renown went to that hermitage, wishing to see his great-souled household priest.
entries.51.4: 'And he saw that great sage, like the sun and blazing as it were with splendour, seated at Vasishtha's left hand.
entries.51.5: 'Humbly he saluted those two, best of ascetics; and by them the king was honoured with welcome and a seat,
entries.51.6: 'with water for the feet and with fruit and root, and he stayed there with the sages.
entries.51.7: 'And as they sat there, sweet talk of many kinds passed among those great sages until the sun stood at noon.
entries.51.8: 'Then in the course of some story the king with joined palms and in courtesy said to that great-souled son of Atri, rich in penance:
entries.51.9: '"Venerable one, how far shall my line endure? And what is my life-span, and Rama's, and what of my other sons?
entries.51.10: '"And of the sons who shall be Rama's, how long shall their life be? Tell me graciously, venerable one, the course of this line of mine."
entries.51.11: 'Hearing those words spoken by King Dasharatha, Durvasa of great splendour began to speak:
entries.51.12: '"Hear, king, what happened of old in the war of the gods and asuras. The daityas, being harried by the gods, took refuge with Bhrigu's wife.
entries.51.13: '"Seeing them taken under her protection, the lord of the gods in wrath struck off the head of Bhrigu's wife with his keen-edged discus.
entries.51.14: '"Then, seeing his wife so slain, the upholder of Bhrigu's line in sudden anger cursed Vishnu, the crusher of the enemy's line:
entries.51.15: '"'Since in a swoon of anger you have slain my wife, who ought not to have been slain, therefore, Janardana, you shall be born in the world of men.
entries.51.16: '"'And there you shall suffer separation from your wife for many years.'
entries.51.17: '"His mind stricken by that curse, he was left to himself in thought.
entries.51.18: '"And Bhrigu, pained by his own cursing, then worshipped that god; and being propitiated by his penance, that god who loves his devotees spoke, and for the good of the worlds he said he would accept that curse.
entries.51.19: '"Thus cursed by Bhrigu in a former birth, that one of great splendour has come here to be your son, best of kings,
entries.51.20: '"renowned in the three worlds by the name of Rama, giver of honour. And he shall reap that great fruit brought about by Bhrigu's curse.
entries.51.21: '"Rama shall be lord of Ayodhya for a long time, and those who follow him shall be happy and prosperous.
entries.51.22: '"Ten thousand years and a thousand years shall Rama rule the kingdom, and then he shall go to the world of Brahma.
entries.51.23: '"And that unconquerable one shall sacrifice with rich horse-sacrifices and shall establish many royal lines.
entries.51.24: '"And two sons shall be born to Raghava of Sita — but elsewhere and not in Ayodhya; this is true and beyond doubt.
entries.51.25: '"And thereafter Raghava shall consecrate those two sons of Sita."
entries.51.26: 'And having told all the coming and going of the king's line, that great sage sat silent.
entries.51.27: 'And when the sage had fallen silent, King Dasharatha saluted those two great souls and returned to his fine city.
entries.51.28: 'This word was spoken by the sage there of old, and I heard it and laid it up in my heart; and it will not be otherwise.
entries.51.29: 'So it being thus, you should not grieve, Raghava. Be firm, best of men, for Sita's sake and for Raghava's.'
entries.51.30: Hearing that most wonderful word spoken by the charioteer, he felt a joy beyond compare and said, 'Well said, well said.'
entries.51.31: Then, as the charioteer and Lakshmana spoke thus upon the road, the sun set and they passed the night in Keshini.
entries.52.1: Having spent that night in Keshini, Lakshmana, delight of the Raghus, rose again at dawn and went on his way.
entries.52.2: Then at midday that great warrior entered Ayodhya, full of jewels and thronged with glad and thriving people.
entries.52.3: But that most wise son of Sumitra fell into the deepest wretchedness: 'Coming to Rama's feet, what shall I say?'
entries.52.4: And as he pondered so, the most noble house of Rama, bright as the moon, appeared before him.
entries.52.5: Getting down from that fine chariot at the door of the royal house, with his face bent down and his mind wretched, he entered unhindered.
entries.52.6: And there he saw Raghava wretched, seated upon his high seat, and beheld his elder brother before him with eyes full of tears.
entries.52.7: Lakshmana with a wretched heart took hold of his feet and said with joined palms and full attention, in a wretched voice:
entries.52.8: 'Putting my noble brother's command before me, I have left the daughter of Janaka upon Ganga's bank as was appointed, at the holy hermitage of Valmiki.
entries.52.9: 'Having left that glorious one of pure conduct near the hermitage, hero, I have come again to serve at your feet.
entries.52.10: 'Do not grieve, tiger among men; such is the way of time. Men of understanding and spirit, such as you, do not grieve.
entries.52.11: 'All gathering ends in loss, all rising ends in falling; all meeting ends in parting, and life ends in death.
entries.52.12: 'Therefore in sons and wives and friends and wealth no excessive attachment should be made, for parting from them is certain.
entries.52.13: 'You are able by your mind alone to master yourself and all the worlds, Kakutstha; how much more your own grief?
entries.52.14: 'Bulls among men such as you are not bewildered in such things. And that reproach, Raghava, will come again.
entries.52.15: 'The very reproach for whose sake Maithili was abandoned in fear of it, king — that reproach will arise in the city; there is no doubt.
entries.52.16: 'So do you, tiger among men, be steadied with firmness; cast off this weak thought and do not grieve.'
entries.52.17: Being addressed thus by the great-souled Lakshmana, Kakutstha, who loves his friends, said with the highest affection to Sumitra's son:
entries.52.18: 'It is so, best of men, as you say, Lakshmana. And I am satisfied, hero, in the carrying out of my charge.
entries.52.19: 'Peace has come, gentle one, and my anguish is set aside. By your fair words I have been won over, Lakshmana.'
entries.53.1: Hearing that most wonderful word of Lakshmana, Rama was well pleased and said this:
entries.53.2: 'Such a kinsman is hard to come by, and in this age especially — such as you are, gentle one, great of understanding and following my own mind.
entries.53.3: 'And whatever is in my heart, you of auspicious marks, hear it; and having heard, do as I say.
entries.53.4: 'Four days have gone, gentle one, in which I have not done the business of the citizens, Sumitra's son; and that cuts my vitals.
entries.53.5: 'Let the people be summoned, and the household priest and the ministers, and the men and women who come with business, bull among men.
entries.53.6: 'For the king who does not do the business of the citizens day by day falls into a dark and dreadful hell; there is no doubt in this.
entries.53.7: 'It is heard that of old there was a king named Nriga of great renown, a guardian of the earth, devoted to brahmins, truthful of speech and pure.
entries.53.8: 'And once that god among men gave to the gods upon earth, at Pushkara, tens of millions of cows adorned with gold, together with their calves.
entries.53.9: 'Then one cow with her calf strayed from the herd and was given unknowingly, sinless one, to a poor brahmin who kept the sacred fires and lived by gleaning.
entries.53.10: 'And her owner, afflicted by hunger, sought his lost cow here and there and could not find her in all the kingdoms for many years.
entries.53.11: 'Then, going to Kanakhala, he saw his own cow in a brahmin's house, her calf now grown old, though she herself was well.
entries.53.12: 'And that brahmin called her by the name he had given her, "Come, Shabala!" — and the cow heard that voice.
entries.53.13: 'Knowing the voice of that hungry brahmin, the cow followed after him as he went, radiant as fire.
entries.53.14: 'And the brahmin who was keeping her ran quickly after the cow and, coming to that sage, said in haste, "This cow is mine.
entries.53.15: '"She was given to me by that lion among kings, Nriga." Then there arose a great dispute between those two learned brahmins.
entries.53.16: 'Disputing with one another, they went to the giver; but coming to the door of the royal house, they were not admitted to Nriga's presence.
entries.53.17: 'Staying there many days and nights, they grew angry; and those two great-souled ones, best of brahmins, being enraged and having waited to the utmost, spoke a word of dreadful purport:
entries.53.18: '"Since you do not give audience even for the accomplishing of suitors' business, you shall become a lizard, invisible to all beings.
entries.53.19: '"For many thousands of years and many hundreds of years you shall dwell a long while as a lizard in this pit.
entries.53.20: '"There shall be born in this world one who increases the fame of the Yadus, renowned as Vasudeva, Vishnu in the form of a man.
entries.53.21: '"He shall free you from that curse, king; and at that time your release shall be accomplished.
entries.53.22: '"For the lifting of the earth's burden, Nara and Narayana both, of great valour, shall be born when the age of Kali is at hand."
entries.53.23: 'Having loosed that curse, those two brahmins were freed of their heat, and they gave that weak old cow to a brahmin.
entries.53.24: 'And so that king suffers that most dreadful curse.
entries.53.25: 'For the slighting of those who come with business turns to fault in kings. Therefore let those with business come swiftly into my presence.
entries.53.26: 'A king does not lose the fruit of a work well done. Go therefore, Sumitra's son, and see who waits with business.'
entries.54.1: Hearing Rama's words, Lakshmana, knower of the highest truth, said with joined palms to Raghava of blazing splendour:
entries.54.2: 'For a small offence, Kakutstha, such a curse was laid by those two brahmins upon the royal sage Nriga — a great curse, like a second staff of Yama.
entries.54.3: 'And hearing himself joined with sin, bull among men, what did King Nriga say to those two angry brahmins?'
entries.54.4: Being addressed thus by Lakshmana, Raghava said again: 'Hear, gentle one, what that king first did when he was stricken by the curse.
entries.54.5: 'When those two brahmins had gone upon their way, Nriga learned of it; and calling all his ministers, the chief men of the city and the household priests,
entries.54.6: 'King Nriga, wholly overcome with sorrow, said to them and to all his people, "Hear me with full attention.
entries.54.7: '"Narada and Parvata, having given me great fear, have gone to the three worlds, those two blameless and gracious ones, in the form of wind.
entries.54.8: '"This prince named Vasu, this godlike one, let him be consecrated today. And let the craftsmen make me a pit whose touch is pleasant,
entries.54.9: '"where I may wear away the curse that came from the mouth of brahmins. Let the craftsmen make one pit that keeps off rain, another that keeps off cold,
entries.54.10: '"and one that keeps off heat and is pleasant to the touch. And whatever trees bear fruit and whatever creepers bear flower,
entries.54.11: '"let these be planted, and shady bushes of many kinds; and let the ground about those pits be made lovely on every side.
entries.54.12: '"There I shall dwell in ease until the turning of time is complete. And let fragrant flowers be set there always,
entries.54.13: '"so that they surround me for a yojana and a half about."
entries.54.14: 'Having made that arrangement, he then instructed Vasu: "Constant in dharma, my son, protect the people by the law of the kshatriya.
entries.54.15: '"You saw yourself how the curse was laid upon me by those two brahmins, best of men, when they were in wrath, and for such an offence as that.
entries.54.16: '"Do not give your body to grief for my sake, bull among men. Fate is a skilful thing, my son, by which I have been brought to calamity.
entries.54.17: '"A man attains only what is to be attained, and goes only where he must go; he gains only what is to be gained, both sorrows and joys.
entries.54.18: '"These are from a former birth, my child; do not despair."
entries.54.19: 'Having spoken thus to his son there, that king of great renown went to that well-made pit to dwell in it, bull among men.
entries.54.20: 'And so entering that pit adorned with great jewels, that great-souled king then wore out the curse that had been loosed in anger by those two brahmins.'
entries.55.1: 'This account of Nriga's curse has been told you by me at length. If you have any desire to hear, listen now to another tale.'
entries.55.2: Being addressed thus by Rama, Sumitra's son said again, 'I have no satiety, king, of these tales that are full of wonder.'
entries.55.3: Being addressed thus by Lakshmana, Rama, delight of the Ikshvakus, began to relate a tale most full of dharma.
entries.55.4: 'There was a king named Nimi among the great-souled Ikshvakus, the twelfth son, established in valour and in dharma.
entries.55.5: 'That king, endowed with valour, founded a city like the city of the gods, near the hermitage of Gautama.
entries.55.6: 'The fair name of that city is heard as Vaijayanta, where the royal sage Nimi of great renown made his dwelling.
entries.55.7: 'And having founded that great city, this thought arose in him: "Let me sacrifice with a long session, and gladden my father's heart."
entries.55.8: 'Then, having invited his father Ikshvaku, the son of Manu, he first chose Vasishtha, best of brahmarshis.
entries.55.9: 'And after him that royal sage Nimi, delight of the Ikshvakus, chose Atri and Angiras and Bhrigu rich in penance.
entries.55.10: 'But Vasishtha said to Nimi, best of royal sages, "I have been chosen before by Indra; wait for an interval."
entries.55.11: 'Then the great brahmin Gautama filled that place, and Vasishtha of great splendour performed Indra's sacrifice.
entries.55.12: 'And King Nimi, having gathered those brahmins, sacrificed upon the slope of Himavat near his own city; and the king remained under consecration five thousand years.
entries.55.13: 'And at the ending of Indra's sacrifice the venerable sage Vasishtha, the blameless one, came into the king's presence to perform the office of hotri.
entries.55.14: 'And there he saw that the interval had been filled by Gautama; and Vasishtha, the son of Brahma, was seized with a great anger.
entries.55.15: 'He sat a moment wishing to see the king; but on that day the royal sage was deeply overcome by sleep.
entries.55.16: 'Then the wrath of the great-souled Vasishtha appeared, and at not seeing the royal sage he began to speak:
entries.55.17: '"Since you have slighted me and chosen another, king, your body shall be without consciousness."
entries.55.18: 'Then the royal sage awoke and, hearing the curse that had been uttered, in a swoon of anger and passion said to that son of Brahma:
entries.55.19: '"I was asleep and knew nothing; yet you, darkened with anger, have loosed upon me the fire of a curse, like a second staff of Yama.
entries.55.20: '"Therefore your body too, brahmarshi, fair as it is, shall be made without consciousness; there is no doubt of it."
entries.55.21: Thus in the power of wrath those two, the king and the best of brahmins, cursed one another then; and suddenly both became bodiless, though the power they had attained remained the same.
entries.56.1: Hearing Rama's words, Lakshmana, slayer of enemy heroes, said with joined palms to Raghava of blazing splendour:
entries.56.2: 'Having laid aside their bodies, Kakutstha, how did those two, the brahmin and the king, honoured of the gods, come again to be joined with a body?'
entries.56.3: Being addressed thus by Lakshmana, Rama, delight of the Ikshvakus, of great splendour and best of men, answered Lakshmana:
entries.56.4: 'Those two righteous ones, having cast off their bodies by each other's curse, the royal sage and the brahmin sage rich in penance, became as the wind.
entries.56.5: 'Being without a body and seeking another, the great sage Vasishtha of great splendour went into his father's presence.
entries.56.6: 'That knower of dharma saluted the feet of the god of gods and, being in the form of wind, said this to the Grandsire:
entries.56.7: '"Venerable one, by Nimi's curse I have become bodiless. Lord of the worlds, great god — you are the egg-born and you are the lotus-born.
entries.56.8: '"For all who are without a body there is great sorrow; and all the works of one who lacks a body are lost, lord. Show me favour, then, for the gaining of another body."
entries.56.9: 'Then Brahma the self-born, of measureless splendour, said to him: "Enter the splendour born of Mitra and Varuna, greatly renowned one.
entries.56.10: '"There too you shall be born of no womb, best of brahmins; and joined with great dharma you shall come again beneath my sway."
entries.56.11: 'Being addressed thus by the god, he saluted the Grandsire and went round him, and set out swiftly for Varuna's dwelling.
entries.56.12: 'At that very time Mitra too was holding the station of Varuna, dwelling with the Ocean of Milk and honoured by the best of the gods.
entries.56.13: 'And at that very time the highest of apsaras, Urvashi, came by chance to that place, surrounded by her companions.
entries.56.14: 'Seeing her endowed with beauty and sporting in Varuna's dwelling, the greatest delight entered Varuna for Urvashi's sake.
entries.56.15: 'And Varuna chose that best of apsaras, whose eyes were lotus-petals and whose face was like the full moon, for union.
entries.56.16: 'Then she stood with joined palms and answered Varuna: "I have already been chosen by Mitra himself, lord of the gods."
entries.56.17: 'And Varuna, pierced by the arrows of Kandarpa, said: "Then I shall let fall this seed of mine into this jar made by the gods.
entries.56.18: '"Letting it fall thus into you, fair-hipped and lovely one, I shall have my desire fulfilled, if you do not wish for union."
entries.56.19: 'Hearing that fair speech of Varuna, guardian of the world, Urvashi was greatly pleased and said:
entries.56.20: '"Let it be so, then. My heart is set upon you and my inclination is rather toward you; but this body, lord, is Mitra's."
entries.56.21: 'Being addressed thus by Urvashi, he let that great and wondrous seed, bright as a blazing tongue of flame, fall into that jar.
entries.56.22: 'And Urvashi went then to where the god Mitra was; and Mitra, coming to her, said this to Urvashi:
entries.56.23: '"You were chosen by me before; why then did you give yourself away? You have chosen another husband, and so you are of ill conduct.
entries.56.24: '"By this ill deed, and defiled by my anger, you shall go to the world of men and dwell there for some time.
entries.56.25: '"There is a royal sage, Pururavas the king of Kashi, son of Budha. Go to him today, foolish one; he shall be your husband."
entries.56.26: 'Then by the fault of that curse she went to Pururavas, the true-born son of Budha.
entries.56.27: 'And of her was born to him a glorious and mighty son, Ayus; and his son was Nahusha, radiant as Indra —
entries.56.28: 'he by whom the lordship of Indra was held for a hundred thousand years, when the lord of the third heaven wandered bewildered after loosing his thunderbolt upon Vritra.
entries.56.29: 'So by that curse Urvashi of fair teeth and fair eyes came to the earth; and that lovely-browed one dwelt there many years, and when the curse was spent she went again to Indra's hall.'
entries.57.1: Hearing that divine tale of wondrous seeming, Lakshmana in the highest pleasure said to Raghava:
entries.57.2: 'Having laid aside their bodies, Kakutstha, how did those two, the brahmin and the king, honoured of the gods, come again to be joined with a body?'
entries.57.3: Hearing that speech of his, Rama of true valour told the tale of the great-souled Vasishtha:
entries.57.4: 'That jar, best of the Raghus, which was filled with the splendour of those two great-souled ones — in it were born those two brahmins full of splendour, best of sages.
entries.57.5: 'There the venerable sage Agastya came into being first; and saying, "I am not your son," he withdrew from Mitra.
entries.57.6: 'And that splendour of Mitra which had been placed before in Urvashi came together in that jar where the seed of Varuna was.
entries.57.7: 'And after some time Vasishtha, born of Mitra and Varuna and endowed with splendour, came into being, the deity of the Ikshvaku line.
entries.57.8: 'And Ikshvaku of great splendour, as soon as that blameless one was born, chose him as household priest, gentle one, for the welfare of this our line.
entries.57.9: 'So the coming forth of the great-souled Vasishtha with a body not his own has been told, gentle one. Hear now what befell Nimi.
entries.57.10: 'Seeing the king bodiless, all those wise sages joined him to the consecration of the sacrifice.
entries.57.11: 'And those best of brahmins, with the citizens and the servants, guarded that body of the lord of men with perfumes and garlands and garments.
entries.57.12: 'Then, when the sacrifice was ended, Bhrigu said there: "I am pleased with you, king; I shall bring back your consciousness."
entries.57.13: 'And all the gods, well pleased, said to Nimi's consciousness: "Choose a boon, royal sage; let it be declared where your consciousness shall dwell."
entries.57.14: 'Being addressed thus by all the gods, the consciousness of Nimi said: "Let me dwell in the eyes of all beings, best of the gods."
entries.57.15: '"So be it," said the gods then to Nimi's consciousness. "You shall move in the eyes of all beings in the form of wind.
entries.57.16: '"And for your sake the eyes of creatures shall blink, lord of earth, that as you move in the form of wind you may have rest again and again."
entries.57.17: 'Having spoken thus, all the gods went as they had come; and the great-souled sages took up Nimi's body.
entries.57.18: 'Placing the fire-sticks there, those great-souled ones churned them with all their strength, with mantras and oblations, for the sake of a son for Nimi.
entries.57.19: 'And as the fire-stick was churned, one of great penance came forth. From the churning they called him Mithi, and from his being born he became Janaka; and since he was born of the bodiless one, he was called Vaideha thereafter.
entries.57.20: 'Thus Janaka was the first king of Videha; and that one of great splendour was named Mithi, and from him this line became Maithila.'
entries.58.1: As Rama spoke thus, Lakshmana, slayer of enemy heroes, answered that great-souled one who blazed as it were with splendour:
entries.58.2: 'It is a great and wondrous marvel, the ancient tale of Videha, tiger among kings, that came to pass between Vasishtha and Nimi.
entries.58.3: 'For Nimi was a kshatriya and brave and moreover under consecration; yet that king showed no forbearance toward the great-souled Vasishtha.'
entries.58.4: Being addressed thus by him, that glorious bull among kshatriyas said to Lakshmana, who was skilled in all the sciences —
entries.58.5: Rama, best of those who take delight, said to his brother of blazing splendour: 'Forbearance is not seen everywhere among men, hero.
entries.58.6: 'Anger is hard to bear, Sumitra's son; yet hear with attention how it was borne by Yayati, keeping the following of courage before you.
entries.58.7: 'King Yayati, son of Nahusha, increaser of the line of Puru — he had two wives, gentle one, unmatched in beauty upon the earth.
entries.58.8: 'One of that royal sage, the son of Nahusha, was preferred by him: Sharmishtha, a daughter of the daityas, the child of Vrishaparvan.
entries.58.9: 'The other was the daughter of Ushanas and the wife of Yayati, bull among men — Devayani of the fair waist; but she was not dear to the king.
entries.58.10: 'And of them were born two sons, beautiful and well made: Sharmishtha bore Puru, and Devayani bore Yadu.
entries.58.11: 'And Puru was dear to the king both for his own qualities and for his mother's sake. Then Yadu, filled with sorrow, said to his mother:
entries.58.12: '"You were born in the family of that god of the line of Bhrigu, whose deeds are done without effort; yet you endure a sorrow in your heart and an insult hard to bear.
entries.58.13: '"Let us two enter the fire together, lady; and let the king take his pleasure many nights with the daughter of the daityas.
entries.58.14: '"Or if it is to be borne by you, then you should give me leave. Forbear, but I shall not forbear; I shall die, and of that there is no doubt."
entries.58.15: 'Hearing her son's words as he wept in the deepest distress, Devayani in anger called her father to mind.
entries.58.16: 'Knowing that summons of his daughter's, the son of Bhrigu came swiftly to where Devayani was.
entries.58.17: 'And seeing her unwell, joyless and as though senseless, her father said to his daughter, "What is this?"
entries.58.18: 'And to the son of Bhrigu of blazing splendour, as he asked her again and again, Devayani in her wrath said:
entries.58.19: '"I shall have recourse to fire, or to sharp poison, or to water, best of sages; I shall eat it or enter it, and I shall not be able to live.
entries.58.20: '"Do not disregard me, wretched and dishonoured. When a tree is slighted, brahmin, those who live by the tree are cut down.
entries.58.21: '"That royal sage slights and despises me, son of Bhrigu, and holds me of no account."
entries.58.22: 'Hearing those words of hers, the son of Bhrigu was flooded with anger and began to speak concerning the son of Nahusha:
entries.58.23: '"Since you slight me, son of Nahusha, being evil-souled, therefore you shall be worn out with a great old age and come to feebleness."
entries.58.24: 'Having spoken thus to his daughter and comforted her, that greatly renowned brahmarshi went again to his own dwelling.
entries.58.25: 'Having spoken thus, that foremost of the best of brahmins, having comforted his daughter Devayani, went back again, radiant as the sun, having given a curse to the son of Nahusha.'
entries.59.1: 'Hearing that Ushanas was angered, the son of Nahusha in his distress, coming to a great old age, said to Yadu:
entries.59.2: '"Yadu, you are a knower of dharma; take this old age for me. Take this great old age, my son, that I may enjoy pleasures, greatly renowned one.
entries.59.3: '"For I am not yet satisfied in the objects of the senses, bull among men. When I have enjoyed my desire, then I shall take back that old age."
entries.59.4: 'Hearing his words, Yadu answered that bull among men: "Let your dear son Puru take that old age.
entries.59.5: '"I am cast out from your favour and from your nearness, lord of earth. Let him take it, king — he who eats beside you shares with you."
entries.59.6: 'Hearing those words of his, the king said to Puru: "Take this old age for me, mighty-armed one."
entries.59.7: 'Being addressed thus by the son of Nahusha, Puru said with joined palms: "I am blessed, I am favoured; I stand within your command."
entries.59.8: 'Knowing Puru's word, the son of Nahusha with the highest gladness felt a joy beyond compare and passed that old age to him.
entries.59.9: 'Then that king, being young again, gained sacrifices by the thousand and ruled the earth many thousands of years.
entries.59.10: 'Then after a long time the king said to Puru: "Bring me that old age, my son; return my deposit to me.
entries.59.11: '"It was as a deposit that I placed that old age upon you, my son; and therefore I shall take it back. Do not be distressed.
entries.59.12: '"And I am pleased, mighty-armed one, at your acceptance of my command; and being pleased I shall consecrate you as lord of men."
entries.59.13: 'Having said this to his son Puru, King Yayati, son of Nahusha, said in anger to Devayani's son:
entries.59.14: '"You were born of me as a son in form, but you are an unassailable rakshasa. Since you set aside my command, be fruitless in offspring.
entries.59.15: '"Since you slight me, your father and as a teacher to you, you shall beget dreadful rakshasas and yatudhanas.
entries.59.16: '"And the line of that evil-minded one shall not stand within the line born of the lunar race; and your line too shall be as ill-conducted as yourself."
entries.59.17: 'Having said this to Puru, the increaser of his kingdom, that royal sage honoured him with consecration and entered a hermitage.
entries.59.18: 'Then after a long time King Yayati, son of Nahusha, came to his appointed end and went to the third heaven.
entries.59.19: 'And Puru of great renown, joined with great dharma, ruled that kingdom in Pratishthana, the finest city of the kingdom of Kashi.
entries.59.20: 'And Yadu, cast out from the royal line, begot yatudhanas by the thousand in the fastness of the city of Krauncha's wood.
entries.59.21: 'This curse loosed by Ushanas was borne by Yayati with the dharma of a kshatriya, whereas Nimi did not bear it so.
entries.59.22: 'All this that I have told you is the way of those who do everything. Let us follow it too, gentle one, so that no fault come to us as it came to Nriga.'
entries.59.23: As Rama with the face of the moon was telling this, the stars grew thin in the sky, and the eastern quarter shone red with the rays of dawn, like a cloth spread out and dyed with the essence of flowers.
entries.60.1: As those two, Rama and Lakshmana, were speaking thus, the night of spring came on, neither cold nor giving heat.
entries.60.2: Then when the dawn was clear and he had done the rites of the forenoon, Kakutstha, who knew the business of the citizens, came to the audience.
entries.60.3: Then Sumantra came and said to Raghava: 'These ascetics stand at the door, king, being held back.
entries.60.4: 'Putting Chyavana of Bhrigu's line before them, those great sages press for the sight of you, great king, being in haste; and they are well disposed toward you, tiger among men — those who dwell upon the bank of the Yamuna.'
entries.60.5: Hearing those words of his, Rama, who knows dharma, said: 'Let those greatly blessed brahmins be brought in, with Bhargava at their head.'
entries.60.6: Putting the king's command before him, the doorkeeper set his palms upon his head and brought in those ascetics, hard to approach.
entries.60.7: More than a hundred of those great-souled ascetics, blazing with their own splendour, entered the royal house.
entries.60.8: And those brahmins, taking full jars honoured with the waters of all the holy fords, brought much fruit and root to Rama.
entries.60.9: And Rama received all of it with affection — all the waters of the holy fords and the fruits of many kinds —
entries.60.10: and that mighty-armed one said to all those great sages: 'Here are the finest of seats; be seated as befits each of you.'
entries.60.11: Hearing Rama's word, all those great sages sat down upon those fair seats of gold called brisis.
entries.60.12: Seeing the sages seated there, that conqueror of his enemies' cities, Raghava, with restraint and with joined palms, spoke:
entries.60.13: 'What is the business of your coming? What may I do for you with full attention? I am to be commanded by the great sages, and I shall fulfil every wish gladly.
entries.60.14: 'This whole kingdom, and the life that dwells in my heart — all this is for the brahmins. I tell you this truly.'
entries.60.15: Hearing those words of his, a great cry of approval went up from those sages of fierce penance who dwell upon the Yamuna's bank.
entries.60.16: And those great-souled ones, filled with great gladness, said: 'This befits you alone upon earth, best of men, and no other.
entries.60.17: 'Many mighty kings have passed away, king, who, weighing the gravity of the matter, would not consent to such a promise.
entries.60.18: 'But you, out of reverence for brahmins, have made this promise without weighing the cause; and you will fulfil it too, there is no doubt. You should save the sages from a great fear.'
entries.61.1: As the sages spoke thus, Kakutstha said: 'Tell me what is to be done, sages; let your fear be gone at once.'
entries.61.2: As Kakutstha spoke so, Bhargava said: 'Hear, lord of men, what is the root of the fears of this land.
entries.61.3: 'Long ago in the Krita age, king, there was a mighty son of Diti, the eldest son of Lola, a great asura named Madhu.
entries.61.4: 'He was devoted to brahmins and a giver of refuge, settled in understanding; and the most generous of the gods had an affection for him beyond compare.
entries.61.5: 'That Madhu, endowed with valour and well established in dharma, performed penance for many thousands of years to please Rudra.
entries.61.6: 'And Rudra was pleased with him and went to give him a boon; and out of great regard a wondrous boon was given him by Rudra.
entries.61.7: 'Drawing from his own trident a trident of great power and great splendour, that great one, well pleased, gave it to him and said:
entries.61.8: '"You have done this matchless dharma which has won my favour. Filled with the highest affection, I give you this excellent weapon.
entries.61.9: '"So long as you do not set yourself against the gods and the brahmins, great asura, this trident shall be yours; otherwise it will come to nothing.
entries.61.10: '"And whoever shall challenge you to battle without fear, this trident shall reduce him to ashes and return again to your hand."
entries.61.11: 'Having won that boon from Rudra, that great asura bowed once more to the great god and said:
entries.61.12: '"Venerable one, let this matchless trident belong always to my line, god; for you are the lord of the gods."
entries.61.13: 'To Madhu speaking thus, the god Shiva, lord of all beings, of great splendour, answered: "That shall not be.
entries.61.14: '"Yet let not this auspicious word of yours, won by my favour, be in vain. One son of yours shall have this trident.
entries.61.15: '"So long as this trident is in your son's hand, he shall be unslayable by all beings, being trident-bearer."
entries.61.16: 'Having thus won a great and wondrous boon from the god, that best of asuras had a splendid dwelling built.
entries.61.17: 'His wife was the greatly blessed and beloved Kumbhinasi, of great radiance, the child of Vishvavasu by Anala.
entries.61.18: 'Her son was of great might and dreadful, named Lavana, who from childhood was evil-souled and did only sinful deeds.
entries.61.19: 'And Madhu, seeing that ill-conducted son, was filled with anger and fell into grief, and said nothing at all to him.
entries.61.20: 'And leaving this world he entered the dwelling of Varuna, and having placed the trident with Lavana he told him of the boon.
entries.61.21: 'And by the power of that trident and by his own wickedness he torments the three worlds, and the ascetics above all.
entries.61.22: 'Such is the power of Lavana and such the trident, Kakutstha. Having heard the measure of it, you are our highest refuge.
entries.61.23: 'Many kings, Rama, have been asked for safety before now by sages tormented with fear; yet we find no protector, hero.
entries.61.24: 'We have heard that Ravana was slain with his forces and his mounts; and so, dear one, we know no other lord of men upon earth for our protector. We wish therefore to be saved, being oppressed with fear of Lavana.
entries.61.25: 'So, Rama, the cause of our fear that has arisen is laid before you. You are able to turn it aside; fulfil that wish, one of undiminished valour.'
entries.62.1: Being addressed thus, Rama said to those sages with joined palms: 'What is Lavana's food, what his manner of life, and where does he dwell?'
entries.62.2: Hearing Raghava's words, all those sages then told how Lavana had grown:
entries.62.3: 'His food is all living beings, and ascetics above all; his manner is cruelty always, and his dwelling is in the wood of Madhu.
entries.62.4: 'Having slain many thousands of lions and tigers, deer and elephants, and men besides, he makes his daily meal of them.
entries.62.5: 'And then that mighty one devours other creatures between whiles, like Antaka with his mouth agape when the dissolution has come.'
entries.62.6: Hearing this, Raghava said to those great sages: 'I shall have that rakshasa slain; let your fear depart.'
entries.62.7: Having made that promise to those sages of fierce splendour, the delight of the Raghus said to all his brothers gathered there:
entries.62.8: 'What hero shall slay Lavana? To whom shall this portion be given — to the mighty-armed Bharata or to the wise Shatrughna?'
entries.62.9: Being addressed thus by Raghava, Bharata said: 'I shall slay him; let that portion be given to me.'
entries.62.10: Hearing Bharata's words, full of steadiness and courage, the younger brother of Lakshmana rose, leaving his golden seat.
entries.62.11: And Shatrughna bowed to the lord of men and said: 'The mighty-armed middle brother, delight of the Raghus, has done his work already.
entries.62.12: 'For my noble brother guarded Ayodhya when it was empty, bearing grief in his heart, waiting for the noble one's return.
entries.62.13: 'And many sorrows were endured by him here, lord of earth; lying upon a bed of sorrow he dwelt in Nandigrama,
entries.62.14: 'eating fruit and root, wearing matted hair and bark. Having endured such sorrow, this delight of the Raghus should suffer no fresh trouble, king, while I stand as your servant.'
entries.62.15: As Shatrughna spoke so, Raghava said again: 'So be it, Kakutstha; let my charge be carried out.
entries.62.16: 'I shall consecrate you in the kingdom, in the fair city of Madhu. Settle Bharata there, mighty-armed one, if it seems good to you.
entries.62.17: 'You are brave and learned, and able for the founding of a city.
entries.62.18: 'For he who uproots an enemy and, when that king is destroyed, sets no king in his place, goes to hell.
entries.62.19: 'So do you slay the son of Madhu, Lavana of sinful resolve, and rule that kingdom in dharma, if you have regard for my word.
entries.62.20: 'And no answer is to be given in the middle of my speech, hero. The command of an elder must be done by the younger; there is no doubt in this.
entries.62.21: 'And receive, Kakutstha, this consecration prepared by me, with rite and mantra, by the brahmins with Vasishtha at their head.'
entries.63.1: Being addressed thus by Rama, Shatrughna, endowed with valour, came to the greatest shame and said slowly:
entries.63.2: 'I see unrighteousness in this matter, Kakutstha, lord of men. How shall the younger be consecrated while the elders stand?
entries.63.3: 'Yet your command must certainly be done, bull among men; and your command, greatly blessed one, is not to be overstepped.
entries.63.4: 'I have heard from you, hero, and I have heard it from the scriptures, that no answer is to be given by me when the middle brother has made his promise.
entries.63.5: 'Yet I uttered that dreadful and unfitting word, "I shall slay Lavana in battle." For such an ill-spoken word may an ill fate be mine, bull among men.
entries.63.6: 'No answer should be given again when the elder has spoken; it is joined with unrighteousness and cuts one off from the world beyond.
entries.63.7: 'So I shall not answer you a second time, Kakutstha. Let no punishment fall upon me a second time, giver of honour.
entries.63.8: 'I am subject to your will, king, bull among men. Take away the unrighteousness done for my sake, Kakutstha, delight of the Raghus.'
entries.63.9: When the brave and great-souled Shatrughna had spoken thus, Rama in gladness said to Bharata and Lakshmana:
entries.63.10: 'Bring the materials of consecration, with full attention. This very day I shall consecrate that tiger among men, Raghava.
entries.63.11: 'And bring at my command the household priest and Kakutstha, and the chief men of the city, the officiants, and all those ministers.'
entries.63.12: Knowing the king's command, those great warriors did so; and putting the household priest at their head, the kings and the brahmins entered the royal house and the preparation of the consecration went forward.
entries.63.13: And so the consecration of the great-souled Shatrughna grew, glorious and giving joy to Raghava and to the city.
entries.63.14: And Shatrughna consecrated shone like the sun, as Skanda of old was consecrated by the hosts of Maruts with Indra among them.
entries.63.15: And when Shatrughna had been consecrated by Rama, whose deeds are done without effort, the citizens rejoiced, and the brahmins learned in many sciences.
entries.63.16: And Kausalya and Sumitra and Kaikeyi performed the rites of blessing in the royal house, and the other royal women too.
entries.63.17: And the great-souled sages who dwell upon Yamuna's bank took Lavana for slain already at Shatrughna's consecration.
entries.63.18: Then Raghava took the consecrated Shatrughna upon his lap and said in sweet words, filling him with splendour:
entries.63.19: 'This unfailing divine arrow is yours, conqueror of enemy cities. With this, gentle delight of the Raghus, you shall slay Lavana.
entries.63.20: 'This arrow was created, Kakutstha, when the self-born unconquered god lay upon the great ocean,
entries.63.21: 'whom neither gods nor asuras could see, being invisible to all beings. By him was this finest of arrows
entries.63.22: 'created in a swoon of anger, for the destruction of those two evil-souled ones, Madhu and Kaitabha, hero, who were bent upon havoc; and wishing to create the three worlds, he slew those two with it in battle.
entries.63.23: 'Having slain them, Kaitabha and Madhu, for the good of all beings, he then made the worlds with this finest of arrows.
entries.63.24: 'This arrow was not loosed by me before, though I sought Ravana's death, Shatrughna, lest it bring a great terror upon living beings.
entries.63.25: 'And as for that great trident of Madhu's, given by the great-souled Tryambaka as the finest of weapons for the destruction of enemies,
entries.63.26: 'he keeps it in his dwelling and worships it again and again, and going to every quarter he obtains the best of food.
entries.63.27: 'But when any, desiring battle, challenges him, then the rakshasa takes up the trident and reduces him to ashes.
entries.63.28: 'So do you, tiger among men, stand at the gate bearing your weapon while he is without his weapon and has not entered the city.
entries.63.29: 'Challenge him to battle, mighty-armed bull among men, while he has not entered his dwelling; then you shall slay that rakshasa.
entries.63.30: 'Done otherwise, he will be unslayable; but if it is done thus, hero, he shall come to destruction.
entries.63.31: 'All this has been told you, and the reverse working of the trident; for the ordinance of the glorious blue-throated one cannot be overpassed.'
entries.64.1: Having spoken thus to Kakutstha and praised him again and again, the delight of the Raghus said yet another thing:
entries.64.2: 'Take these four thousand horses, bull among men, and two thousand chariots and a hundred of the finest elephants;
entries.64.3: 'and let market-rows adorned with wares of many kinds go between them, and dancers and players too, following Kakutstha.
entries.64.4: 'Take a million in gold and silver, bull among men, and go, Shatrughna, with wealth and mounts enough.
entries.64.5: 'And keep your army well fed, hero, glad and thriving and not unruly; win them, best of men, by kindly speech and by giving.
entries.64.6: 'For wealth does not stand by a man there, nor wives nor kinsmen; but a well-pleased body of servants does, wherever you may be, Raghava.
entries.64.7: 'Then, having sent on that great host thronged with glad men, go alone with your bow in hand to the wood of Madhu.
entries.64.8: 'And go so that Lavana, the son of Madhu, does not learn that you are coming in search of battle; go without giving him warning.
entries.64.9: 'For there is no other death for him, bull among men; whoever comes into his sight is slain by Lavana.
entries.64.10: 'And when the hot season has passed and the rainy nights have come, then slay Lavana, gentle one; that is the hour of that evil-minded one.
entries.64.11: 'Let your cooks go forward with the great sages before them, so that they may cross the water of Jahnavi while some of the hot season remains.
entries.64.12: 'Leaving all your force there upon the river's bank, go forward with full attention and swiftly, with your bow alone.'
entries.64.13: Being addressed thus by Rama, Shatrughna called together those mighty commanders of the host and said:
entries.64.14: 'These halting-places have been counted for you; you shall stay where each is appointed. And stay without quarrel, so that none is troubled.'
entries.64.15: Having thus given them their orders and sent forward that great host, he saluted Kausalya and Sumitra and Kaikeyi.
entries.64.16: And going round Rama from left to right and bowing his head to him, with Rama's leave Shatrughna, scorcher of foes,
